idiom_name: status route running registered checks; aggregate HTTP 200/503 plus separate per-signal endpoints (liveness, readiness, deep)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: register named checks - each read-only and individually time-boxed - behind one or more routes on a port the prober can reach. The assignment of checks to endpoints is the design: the liveness endpoint runs only local-invariant checks (event loop responsive, main loop unwedged) because its failing answer restarts the process; the readiness endpoint may run dependency checks because its failing answer only drains traffic; a third deep endpoint reports dependency detail to alerting and is never wired to a prober's routing or restart decision. Aggregate worst-status-wins into 200 healthy / 503 (or 500) unhealthy, with an optional status document naming each check's state and last error behind detail-visibility controls. Every check gets its own deadline shorter than the prober's timeout, checks run in parallel, and the endpoint caps total runtime so one slow dependency cannot make the probe hang - a hung probe is indistinguishable from an unreachable process. Where the prober cannot speak HTTP, surface the same checks as exec hooks, a TCP accept, or the gRPC health service. Keep the endpoint free of auth redirects (or give the prober credentials), free of side effects, and off the request path that real traffic saturates.
code_sketch:
checks = {"db": check_db(timeout=2s), "cache": check_cache(timeout=1s)}

GET /livez:              # restart signal - local state only, no external I/O
  ok = event_loop_responsive(timeout=500ms)
  return 200 if ok else 503

GET /readyz:             # drain signal - dependency checks allowed
  r = await run_parallel([checks["db"], checks["cache"]], budget=2s)
  return (200 if r.all_ok else 503), render(r.summary())

GET /healthz/detail:     # alerting only - never wired to a prober
  return 200, render(run_all(checks))   # names the failing dependency
pitfalls: Wrong move: point the liveness probe (or the load balancer) at the one deep /health that pings database, cache and queues -> every instance fails in lockstep the moment a shared dependency blips, restarts or drains together, and the reconnection storm of the recovering fleet deepens the original outage -> give liveness a local-only endpoint, let only readiness consider dependencies (drain, never restart), and send deep checks to alerting.

Wrong move: return 200 from a static handler because dependency checks are 'too flaky' -> the endpoint now certifies instances that cannot serve traffic, and the prober keeps routing users to them -> keep the shallow liveness answer honest about the narrow thing it checks, and express dependency truth in readiness and detail endpoints instead of flattening everything into a lie.

Wrong move: run dependency checks without a per-check deadline -> a stalled database makes the probe hang until the prober's own timeout, which the orchestrator reads as a dead process, so slow dependencies trigger exactly the restarts a health endpoint exists to prevent -> cap each check with its own timeout, run checks in parallel, and always answer within the probe budget.

Wrong move: serve the health route from the application's saturated request pipeline -> under load the probe queues behind real traffic, healthy-but-busy instances fail their probes and are killed, shrinking capacity at the worst moment -> serve probes from a lightweight path (management port or dedicated handler) and size thresholds for realistic tail latency, not median latency.

Wrong move: let a readiness check open connections, warm caches or consume a queue message 'to prove it works' -> a poll every few seconds turns a background probe into a repeated production side effect -> checks must be read-only; derive dependency health from cheap reads or state the application already maintains.

Wrong move: expose the full dependency status document to unauthenticated callers because the prober needs 200s from the same URL anyway -> the body leaks hostnames, versions and failure text that map the attack surface -> keep the prober's answer code-only and gate detail behind authentication, a management port or network policy.

Wrong move: tune failureThreshold and timeoutSeconds until the restart storms stop -> higher thresholds only widen the window in which the fleet runs broken (detection time is period times threshold) while the depth-versus-routing flaw remains -> fix signal separation and check depth first, then tune thresholds to measured boot time and GC/pause tails.

Wrong move: give a slow-starting app a liveness probe with no startup gate -> long initialization trips the probe during boot and the runtime restarts the app in an endless loop that never reaches the traffic-serving phase -> add a startup probe (or equivalent gate) that holds liveness and readiness checks off until the first success.
